A direct consequence of our results is a revised interpretation of both the stellar rank and non-Gaussianity itself: when superselection rules are properly taken into account, quadrature non-Gaussianity - and nonzero stellar rank - act as witnesses of particle entanglement, rather than being linked with photon addition to Gaussian states as previously assumed. In addition, we show that because the stellar rank depends on a specific choice of coherent states, its relation to computational resources and potential quantum advantage is inherently basis-dependent, being naturally tied to quadrature eigenstates as the computational basis. Motivated by this observation, we generalize the notion of stellar rank to arbitrary computational bases, thereby establishing it as a genuine witness of bosonic resources that may enable quantum advantage.

AI.tldr: The paper reinterprets non-Gaussianity and stellar rank as witnesses of particle entanglement rather than photon addition, shows stellar rank's basis-dependence, and generalizes it to arbitrary computational bases as a resource for quantum advantage.
AI.motivation: To provide a physical interpretation of non-Gaussianity and connect it to computational resources, challenging previous assumptions about stellar rank's relation to photon addition and revealing its basis-dependent nature.
AI.method: Analyze stellar rank as a limiting case of polynomial roots (Majorana polynomials) representing bosonic states with quantized phase reference. Consider superselection rules to reinterpret non-Gaussianity, and generalize stellar rank to arbitrary computational bases.
AI.result: Quadrature non-Gaussianity and nonzero stellar rank witness particle entanglement (not photon addition). Stellar rank is basis-dependent, naturally tied to quadrature eigenstates. Generalized stellar rank serves as genuine witness of bosonic resources enabling quantum advantage.
AI.conclusion: Non-Gaussianity and stellar rank fundamentally relate to particle entanglement when superselection rules are considered. Stellar rank's computational resource interpretation is basis-dependent, requiring generalization to arbitrary bases to properly characterize bosonic resources for quantum advantage.

title: Entangled photons from quantum-dot-cavity systems under non-Markovian decoherence by pulsed excitation
summary: Cascaded emission from the biexciton state of a quantum dot results in polarization entangled photon pairs. However, modelling this system becomes challenging when photon emission is cavity-mediated due to the large Hilbert space and non-Markovian nature of its phonon-induced decoherence. Here, we introduce an algorithm that reduces the computational cost of the numerically exact process tensor method for non-Markovian dynamics simulations when the environmental coupling operator has degenerate eigenvalues, making calculations of the non-Markovian dynamics of large systems feasible. We compute the degree of entanglement of photon pairs generated by pulsed two-photon resonant excitation and find surprisingly good agreement between the numerically exact results and those calculated using the approximate polaron master equation method, permitting an efficient exploration of trends across system parameters.

AI.tldr: Researchers develop an efficient algorithm for simulating non-Markovian dynamics in large quantum systems with degenerate environmental coupling operators, enabling exact calculations of cavity-mediated biexciton emission and entanglement in quantum dots.
AI.motivation: Cavity-mediated biexciton emission in quantum dots produces polarization-entangled photon pairs, but simulating this system is challenging due to large Hilbert spaces and non-Markovian phonon-induced decoherence. Existing methods are computationally expensive for large systems.
AI.method: Developed an algorithm that reduces computational cost of the numerically exact process tensor method for non-Markovian dynamics when environmental coupling operators have degenerate eigenvalues. Applied this to compute entanglement of photon pairs from pulsed two-photon resonant excitation in quantum dots.
AI.result: The algorithm makes non-Markovian dynamics calculations of large systems feasible. Surprisingly good agreement found between numerically exact results and approximate polaron master equation method for entanglement calculations, enabling efficient parameter exploration.
AI.conclusion: The new algorithm enables exact simulations of large quantum systems with non-Markovian dynamics, validating the polaron master equation approximation for quantum dot entanglement calculations and facilitating efficient parameter optimization.

title: Entanglement in a driven two-qubit system coupled to common cavity
summary: A system, comprised of a qubit pair coupled to a common cavity, is studied with the aim of establishing qubit entanglement. This study is the sequel of the paper Phys. Rev. A 111, 043705 (2025), where similar model was investigated for an initially vacuum cavity. In the present manuscript the cavity with finite initial occupancy is considered and the effect of asymmetric qubit cavity couplings is investigated. For a closed system scenario, the ratio of the qubit-cavity couplings shows a threshold beyond which no maximally-entangled qubit state is available. The threshold value is shown to depend on the excitation level of the cavity. For a driven-dissipative case steady state entanglement is shown to depend non-monotonically on the qubit drive. Intricate interplay of drive, dissipation, and coupling asymmetry is shown to be pivotal for steady-state entanglement generation.

AI.tldr: Study of qubit entanglement in a cavity QED system with finite initial cavity occupancy and asymmetric qubit-cavity couplings, extending previous vacuum cavity research.
AI.motivation: Extend previous research on qubit entanglement in cavity QED systems by considering more realistic scenarios with finite initial cavity occupancy and asymmetric coupling strengths between qubits and the cavity.
AI.method: Analyze a system of two qubits coupled to a common cavity with finite initial excitation and asymmetric qubit-cavity couplings, examining both closed system dynamics and driven-dissipative steady states.
AI.result: For closed systems, a threshold in qubit-cavity coupling ratio exists beyond which maximal entanglement is unattainable, with threshold dependent on cavity excitation level. For driven-dissipative systems, steady-state entanglement shows non-monotonic dependence on qubit drive, with complex interplay between drive, dissipation, and coupling asymmetry.
AI.conclusion: Finite initial cavity occupancy and asymmetric qubit-cavity couplings significantly impact entanglement generation, with threshold behavior in closed systems and complex non-monotonic dependencies in driven-dissipative systems, highlighting the importance of these factors for practical entanglement generation.

title: Proposal for erasure conversion in integer fluxonium qubits
summary: We propose an erasure conversion scheme on the $|e\rangle-|f\rangle$ and $|g\rangle-|f\rangle$ qubits in integer fluxonium qubits (IFQs), which are both first-order insensitive to $1/f$ flux noise. The $|e\rangle-|f\rangle$ transition is identical to that of a usual fluxonium qubit and hence is expected to have excellent coherence time, while the $|g\rangle-|f\rangle$ transition is additionally protected from the energy relaxation by the parity symmetry. The dominant error in both qubits arises due to the energy relaxation: from $|e\rangle$ to $|g\rangle$ in the $e\text{--}f$ qubit and from $|f\rangle$ to $|e\rangle$ in the $g\text{--}f$ qubit. Such errors can be treated as erasure events, and their efficient detection improves the performance of quantum error-correcting codes. We consider a protocol for such erasure conversion based on the dispersive readout. Our main finding is that, with proper circuit parameter choice, carefully designed gate sets, and the integration of erasure conversion, IFQs promise high effective coherence times.

AI.tldr: Erasure conversion scheme for integer fluxonium qubits using |e⟩-|f⟩ and |g⟩-|f⟩ transitions, both insensitive to 1/f flux noise, with efficient erasure detection for quantum error correction.
AI.motivation: To leverage the coherence advantages of integer fluxonium qubits while addressing dominant energy relaxation errors by converting them into detectable erasure events for improved quantum error correction performance.
AI.method: Proposes erasure conversion scheme on |e⟩-|f⟩ and |g⟩-|f⟩ transitions in integer fluxonium qubits, using dispersive readout for detection, with careful circuit parameter selection and gate set design.
AI.result: Both transitions are first-order insensitive to 1/f flux noise; |e⟩-|f⟩ has excellent coherence, |g⟩-|f⟩ has additional parity symmetry protection; dominant energy relaxation errors can be converted to detectable erasures.
AI.conclusion: With proper parameter choice, gate design, and erasure conversion integration, integer fluxonium qubits promise high effective coherence times for quantum computing applications.

title: Lie-algebraic incompleteness of symmetry-adapted VQE for non-Abelian molecular point groups
summary: Symmetry-adapted variational quantum eigensolvers (VQE) based on the Unitary Coupled-Cluster ansatz (SymUCCSD) effectively reduce the parameter count for Abelian molecular point groups, yet they systematically fail for non-Abelian groups without a fully established theoretical explanation. In this work, we prove that the Abelian-subgroup restriction induces a spurious splitting of multidimensional irreducible representations, prematurely discarding cross-component excitations. At the Lie-algebraic level, this filter confines the Dynamical Lie Algebra (DLA) to the Abelian subalgebra $\mathfrak{u}(1)^{d_λ}$, restricting the reachable state manifold to a measure-zero torus $\mathbb{T}^{d_λ}$. However, completing the algebra is insufficient on its own due to a critical numerical trap: when standard molecular orbitals adapted solely to an Abelian subgroup are utilized, cross-component integrals vanish identically, creating an artificial zero-gradient plateau along non-Abelian algebraic directions. Numerical experiments on NH$_3$/STO-3G ($C_{3v}$, 16 qubits) confirm both the predicted DLA confinement and the gradient plateau, with SymUCCSD converging to an error of $21.8$~mHa above the FCI energy despite full optimizer convergence. Our analysis provides a rigorous algebraic and geometric diagnosis for the observed numerical breakdown, establishing that recovering full equivariant dynamics fundamentally necessitates both the inclusion of complete off-diagonal generators and the strategic parametrization of non-Abelian degrees of freedom.

AI.tldr: SymUCCSD VQE fails for non-Abelian molecular groups due to Abelian-subgroup restriction causing spurious splitting of irreducible representations and creating artificial zero-gradient plateaus.
AI.motivation: Symmetry-adapted VQE based on Unitary Coupled-Cluster (SymUCCSD) effectively reduces parameters for Abelian molecular point groups but systematically fails for non-Abelian groups without a clear theoretical explanation.
AI.method: Prove that Abelian-subgroup restriction induces spurious splitting of multidimensional irreducible representations, discarding cross-component excitations. Analyze at Lie-algebraic level showing DLA confinement to Abelian subalgebra, restricting reachable states to measure-zero torus. Identify numerical trap where standard molecular orbitals adapted to Abelian subgroup cause vanishing cross-component integrals and artificial zero-gradient plateaus.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on NH3/STO-3G (C3v, 16 qubits) confirm both predicted DLA confinement and gradient plateau, with SymUCCSD converging to error of 21.8 mHa above FCI energy despite full optimizer convergence.
AI.conclusion: Recovering full equivariant dynamics fundamentally requires both inclusion of complete off-diagonal generators and strategic parametrization of non-Abelian degrees of freedom. Provides rigorous algebraic and geometric diagnosis for numerical breakdown.

title: Robust Quantum Sensing via Prethermal Spin Orbits
summary: Practical performance of quantum sensors is often curtailed by uncontrolled environmental drift (bias-field instability, temperature fluctuations, mechanical vibration), background fields, and imperfect control pulses. This motivates developing physical mechanisms that intrinsically compensate for such perturbations while retaining high sensitivity to target fields. We introduce an interaction-protected magnetometry scheme where periodic driving steers the collective magnetization onto two long-lived, prethermal Floquet "orbit" axes well-separated on the Bloch sphere. Rapid toggling between these axes encodes target fields as a differential signal, whereas background fields appear as common-mode motion that is strongly rejected, achieving >1000-fold suppression while canceling prethermal transients. This enables accurate reconstruction of rapidly varying audio-band magnetic signals without predictive filtering or spectral tuning. We provide an experimental proof-of-principle using a dense ensemble of coupled nuclear spins, operated here as a broadband (0-1 kHz) magnetometer. The protocol is remarkably tolerant to imperfections, operating robustly across millions of pulses under pulse-angle (~10°) and pulse frequency (>1 kHz) errors, large bias-field drifts (>50 $\mathrmμ$T), temperature variations over 150 K, and harsh mechanical vibrations. These results establish Floquet prethermalization as a resource for robust quantum sensors that combines broadband magnetic-field sensitivity with intrinsic immunity to diverse environmental and control perturbations, opening a path toward stable quantum metrology beyond controlled laboratory conditions.

AI.tldr: Interaction-protected magnetometry using Floquet prethermalization achieves broadband magnetic sensing with intrinsic immunity to environmental perturbations through differential encoding between two long-lived prethermal axes.
AI.motivation: Quantum sensors suffer from environmental drift (bias-field instability, temperature fluctuations, vibration), background fields, and imperfect control pulses, limiting practical performance outside controlled lab conditions.
AI.method: Periodic driving steers collective magnetization onto two long-lived prethermal Floquet "orbit" axes separated on Bloch sphere. Rapid toggling between axes encodes target fields as differential signal while background fields appear as common-mode motion that is strongly rejected (>1000× suppression).
AI.result: Experimental proof-of-principle using dense nuclear spin ensemble achieves broadband (0-1 kHz) magnetometry. Protocol tolerates: pulse-angle errors (~10°), pulse frequency errors (>1 kHz), bias-field drifts (>50 μT), temperature variations (150 K), and mechanical vibrations across millions of pulses.
AI.conclusion: Floquet prethermalization enables robust quantum sensors combining broadband magnetic sensitivity with intrinsic immunity to environmental and control perturbations, advancing stable quantum metrology beyond laboratory conditions.

title: Evidential Quantum Vertical Federated Learning
summary: Quantum federated learning (QFL) has recently emerged as a promising paradigm for privacy-preserving collaborative learning, yet most existing studies focus on horizontal federated learning and ignore the vertical federated learning (VFL), where parties hold complementary features of aligned samples. In this work, we propose Evidential Quantum Vertical Federated Learning (eviQVFL), a VFL-tailored QFL framework that employs a hybrid classical-quantum architecture for party-side feature processing, mapping local features into a quantum state. To preserve privacy and avoid information loss, party-side output states are directly transmitted to the server via quantum teleportation, and the server fuses the received quantum states with a non-parametric evidential fusion circuit grounded in evidence theory, followed by measurement-based inference. Extensive simulations on image classification and other real-world datasets demonstrate that eviQVFL consistently achieves higher classification accuracy than other classical and quantum baselines under comparable parameter budgets. Both empirical observations and theoretical analysis indicate that eviQVFL achieve less approximation error with limited quantum resources, while maintaining training stability and offering stronger feature privacy.

AI.tldr: Proposes eviQVFL, a quantum vertical federated learning framework using quantum teleportation for privacy-preserving feature transmission and evidential fusion circuits for server-side processing.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum federated learning research focuses on horizontal settings, ignoring vertical federated learning where parties hold complementary features of aligned samples. There's a need for VFL-tailored quantum approaches that preserve privacy while maintaining accuracy.
AI.method: Hybrid classical-quantum architecture: party-side feature processing maps local features to quantum states, transmitted via quantum teleportation to server. Server uses non-parametric evidential fusion circuit based on evidence theory, followed by measurement-based inference.
AI.result: Extensive simulations on image classification and real-world datasets show eviQVFL achieves higher classification accuracy than classical and quantum baselines under comparable parameter budgets. Achieves less approximation error with limited quantum resources while maintaining training stability and stronger feature privacy.
AI.conclusion: eviQVFL successfully addresses vertical federated learning in quantum settings, demonstrating superior performance, privacy preservation, and resource efficiency compared to existing approaches.

title: A Grid-Based Quantum Algorithm for the Time-Dependent Simulation of Infrared Spectra
summary: We develop a time-dependent, grid-based framework for simulating infrared spectra that is specifically designed for quantum computers. The proposed circuit employs a probabilistic strategy for applying the non-unitary dipole operator and an Split Operator-Quantum Fourier Transform time evolution scheme. Using a vibrational model of the water molecule as a test system, our classical emulation results demonstrate accurate determination of fundamental and overtone band positions and intensities via Fourier-transformed dipole-dipole autocorrelation functions. We also identify the optimal time parameters that minimise gate depths while maintaining high fidelity. For further resource reduction, we validate the feasibility of utilising harmonic oscillator approximations in state preparation and dipole operator truncations. With its scalability to higher-dimensional normal mode spaces, this wavefunction-based approach establishes a robust foundation for studying IR spectra on future quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: A quantum computing framework for simulating infrared spectra using time-dependent grid methods, probabilistic dipole operators, and Split Operator-QFT time evolution, validated on water molecule vibrations.
AI.motivation: To develop a quantum computing approach for simulating infrared spectra that can scale to higher-dimensional normal mode spaces, addressing the computational challenges of classical methods for molecular vibrational spectroscopy.
AI.method: Time-dependent grid-based framework with probabilistic application of non-unitary dipole operator, Split Operator-Quantum Fourier Transform time evolution scheme, using Fourier-transformed dipole-dipole autocorrelation functions, with harmonic oscillator approximations for state preparation and dipole operator truncations.
AI.result: Classical emulation on water molecule vibrations demonstrates accurate determination of fundamental and overtone band positions and intensities, identifies optimal time parameters minimizing gate depths while maintaining high fidelity, and validates feasibility of harmonic oscillator approximations for resource reduction.
AI.conclusion: The wavefunction-based approach establishes a robust foundation for studying IR spectra on future quantum hardware with scalability to higher-dimensional normal mode spaces.

title: A Refined Biorthogonal Framework for Non-Hermitian Quantum Theory and Its Application in Dynamical Phase Transition
summary: The description of states and dynamics in non-Hermitian systems is fundamentally linked to the choice of an appropriate theoretical framework--a point of ongoing debate in the field. This work addresses this issue by proposing a consistent formulation that reconciles existing controversies and establishes a unified theoretical understanding. Our approach rests on a foundational premise: The dynamics of both left- and right-vectors of a non-Hermitian system must satisfy the Schrödinger equation. Building on this physically motivated assumption, we refine the biorthogonal framework, leading to a consistent reformulation of non-Hermitian quantum theory. This refined framework can naturally reduce to standard quantum mechanics in the Hermitian limit. As a concrete application, we analyze the dynamical phase transition in a one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model within this refined framework. Notably, our formulation naturally generalizes the known condition for such transitions in Hermitian two-band systems, namely, $\mathbf{d}_{k}^i\cdot\mathbf{d}_{k}^f=0$, to the non-Hermitian case, where it takes the form $\mathrm{Re}\Bigl[\frac{\mathbf{d}_{k}^i}{d_{k}^i}\cdot\frac{\mathbf{d}_{k}^f}{d_{k}^f}\Bigr]=0$. Furthermore, we identify entirely new dynamical phase transitions that cannot be characterized by the winding number. We hope that this refined framework will find broad applications in the study of non-Hermitian systems.

AI.tldr: A consistent theoretical framework for non-Hermitian quantum systems is proposed, based on requiring both left- and right-vectors to satisfy the Schrödinger equation, which refines the biorthogonal framework and naturally reduces to standard quantum mechanics in the Hermitian limit.
AI.motivation: To resolve ongoing debates about the appropriate theoretical framework for describing states and dynamics in non-Hermitian systems by establishing a consistent formulation that reconciles existing controversies.
AI.method: Refine the biorthogonal framework based on the foundational premise that both left- and right-vectors must satisfy the Schrödinger equation, leading to a consistent reformulation of non-Hermitian quantum theory.
AI.result: The refined framework naturally reduces to standard quantum mechanics in the Hermitian limit and successfully analyzes dynamical phase transitions in a 1D SSH model, generalizing the Hermitian condition $\mathbf{d}_{k}^i\cdot\mathbf{d}_{k}^f=0$ to the non-Hermitian case as $\mathrm{Re}\Bigl[\frac{\mathbf{d}_{k}^i}{d_{k}^i}\cdot\frac{\mathbf{d}_{k}^f}{d_{k}^f}\Bigr]=0$, while identifying new dynamical phase transitions not characterized by winding number.
AI.conclusion: The proposed refined framework provides a consistent theoretical foundation for non-Hermitian quantum systems, reconciles existing controversies, and offers broad applicability for studying non-Hermitian phenomena, including novel dynamical phase transitions beyond winding number characterization.

title: A Quantum Encoding of Traveling Salesperson Tours via Route Generation, Cost Phases, and a Valid-Permutation
summary: We present a compact quantum encoding of the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) based on a time-register representation of tours. A candidate route is represented as a sequence of $n$ city labels over discrete time steps, with one fixed start city and the remaining cities encoded in binary registers. We describe three ingredients of the construction: uniform route generation over the route register, a reversible oracle for marking valid tours, and a phase oracle that encodes the total tour cost. The validity oracle distinguishes permutations of the non-start cities from invalid assignments, while the cost oracle accumulates the contribution of the start edge, intermediate transitions, and return edge into a tour-dependent phase. This yields a coherent superposition of candidate routes with feasibility and tour-length information embedded directly in the quantum state. The number of qubits required is $\Order{n\log_2(n)}$ and the circuit depth scales quadratically in $n$. The encoding is compatible with amplitude amplification or spectral filtering techniques such as the quantum singular value transform (QSVT) or Grover's algorithm. However, due to the exponentially small fraction of valid tours, the overall complexity remains exponential even when combined with amplitude amplification.

AI.tldr: Compact quantum encoding of TSP using time-register representation with O(n log n) qubits, quadratic circuit depth, and compatibility with amplitude amplification techniques, though overall complexity remains exponential.
AI.motivation: To develop an efficient quantum encoding for the Traveling Salesperson Problem that can leverage quantum algorithms like amplitude amplification and QSVT, while maintaining reasonable qubit requirements and circuit depth.
AI.method: Time-register representation of tours with fixed start city and binary registers for remaining cities, featuring uniform route generation, reversible validity oracle for detecting permutations, and phase oracle encoding tour cost through start edge, intermediate transitions, and return edge contributions.
AI.result: Achieves O(n log₂n) qubit requirement and quadratic circuit depth scaling, produces coherent superposition of candidate routes with feasibility and tour-length information embedded in quantum state, compatible with amplitude amplification techniques.
AI.conclusion: The encoding provides a compact quantum representation of TSP suitable for quantum algorithms, but the exponential scarcity of valid tours means overall complexity remains exponential even with amplitude amplification, highlighting fundamental limitations of quantum approaches to combinatorial optimization problems.

title: The Average Relative Entropy and Transpilation Depth determines the noise robustness in Variational Quantum Classifiers
comment: Variational Quantum Classifier, Quantum Machine Learning, Quantum Relative Entropy, Noise Resilient Quantum Circuits, Shallow Circuits
summary: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) have been extensively researched for applications in Quantum Machine Learning (QML), Optimization, and Molecular simulations. Although designed for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, VQAs are predominantly evaluated classically due to uncertain results on noisy devices and limited resource availability. Raising concern over the reproducibility of simulated VQAs on noisy hardware. While prior studies indicate that VQAs may exhibit noise resilience in specific parameterized shallow quantum circuits, there are no definitive measures to establish what defines a shallow circuit or the optimal circuit depth for VQAs on a noisy platform. These challenges extend naturally to Variational Quantum Classification (VQC) algorithms, a subclass of VQAs for supervised learning. In this article, we propose a relative entropy-based metric to verify whether a VQC model would perform similarly on a noisy device as it does on simulations. We establish a strong correlation between the average relative entropy difference in classes, transpilation circuit depth, and their performance difference on a noisy quantum device. Our results further indicate that circuit depth alone is insufficient to characterize shallow circuits. We present empirical evidence to support these assertions across a diverse array of techniques for implementing VQC, datasets, and multiple noisy quantum devices.

AI.tldr: Proposes a relative entropy-based metric to predict whether variational quantum classification models will perform similarly on noisy quantum hardware as in simulations, finding that circuit depth alone is insufficient to characterize shallow circuits.
AI.motivation: Variational quantum algorithms are predominantly evaluated classically despite being designed for NISQ devices, raising concerns about reproducibility on noisy hardware. There are no definitive measures to determine what constitutes a shallow circuit or optimal depth for VQAs on noisy platforms, particularly for variational quantum classification algorithms.
AI.method: Proposes a relative entropy-based metric to verify whether VQC models would perform similarly on noisy devices as in simulations. Analyzes correlation between average relative entropy difference in classes, transpilation circuit depth, and performance difference on noisy quantum devices across diverse VQC implementation techniques, datasets, and multiple noisy quantum devices.
AI.result: Establishes strong correlation between average relative entropy difference in classes, transpilation circuit depth, and their performance difference on noisy quantum devices. Shows circuit depth alone is insufficient to characterize shallow circuits. Provides empirical evidence supporting these assertions across various VQC implementations, datasets, and quantum devices.
AI.conclusion: The proposed relative entropy-based metric helps predict VQC performance on noisy hardware, addressing reproducibility concerns. Circuit depth alone is inadequate for characterizing shallow circuits, suggesting more nuanced metrics are needed for evaluating VQA performance on NISQ devices.

title: Probabilistic theories stable under teleportation
summary: A long-standing problem in the foundations of quantum mechanics is to identify a physical principle that explains why algebraically maximal violations of Bell inequalities can generally not be achieved in Nature. One recently proposed approach considers iterated Bell tests, where a Bell test is performed on a state that has undergone several rounds of entanglement swapping. Obtaining large violations in this scenario is more demanding, because it requires a theory to have both highly entangled states and highly entangled measurements. It has been conjectured that the maximal quantum mechanical Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH)-value of $2\sqrt2$ might be optimal for any probabilistic theory which, like quantum mechanics, maintains its CHSH-value after an arbitrary number of rounds of entanglement swapping. However, in a previous paper, we have exhibited a first example of a probabilistic theory that can sustain a CHSH value of $4$ in this setting. In this work, further investigating this property, we give a classification of all general probabilistic theories (GPTs) whose CHSH value is stable in the above sense. The problem reduces to a representation-theoretic condition that allows for exactly seven solutions. The GPT from our previous work showed some counter-intuitive features, e.g. that the local state space had a higher dimension than seemed necessary to realize CHSH tests. The classification shows that this is necessarily so. Along the way, we generalize the concept of self-testing to GPTs.

AI.tldr: The paper classifies all general probabilistic theories (GPTs) that maintain stable CHSH values through arbitrary rounds of entanglement swapping, finding exactly seven solutions and showing that certain counter-intuitive features are necessary.
AI.motivation: To understand why quantum mechanics cannot achieve maximal algebraic violations of Bell inequalities (CHSH value of 4) and to identify physical principles that explain this limitation, particularly in the context of iterated Bell tests with entanglement swapping.
AI.method: The authors use representation-theoretic analysis to classify all GPTs whose CHSH value remains stable under arbitrary rounds of entanglement swapping. They generalize the concept of self-testing to GPTs and reduce the problem to a representation-theoretic condition.
AI.result: The classification yields exactly seven solutions for GPTs with stable CHSH values. The analysis shows that certain counter-intuitive features observed in previous work (like local state spaces having higher dimensions than necessary for CHSH tests) are necessarily present in such theories.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a complete classification of GPTs with stable CHSH values under entanglement swapping, revealing that only seven such theories exist and that they necessarily exhibit certain non-intuitive properties, advancing the understanding of physical principles limiting Bell inequality violations.

title: Memory-Nonlinearity Trade-off across Quantum Reservoir Computing Frameworks
summary: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) harnesses driven quantum dynamics for time-series processing, yet the mechanisms behind the differing performance levels across its many implementations remain unclear. We show that apparently unrelated approaches-including memory restriction, weak measurements, operation near the edge of quantum chaos, and dissipative dynamics-are in fact governed by the same underlying principle, namely a tunable balance between memory retention and nonlinear response. Using the information processing capacity, a dynamical measure from nonlinear systems theory, we place these behaviors in a unified framework and identify the regimes in which quantum reservoirs surpass the standard protocol. Our results reveal a fundamental connection between memory and nonlinear response. This provides a general design principle for enhanced information processing and enables systematic analysis and optimization inspired by classical dynamical quantifiers.

AI.tldr: Quantum reservoir computing performance variations stem from a tunable balance between memory retention and nonlinear response, unifying diverse approaches through information processing capacity analysis.
AI.motivation: The mechanisms behind differing performance levels across various quantum reservoir computing implementations remain unclear, despite the field's use of driven quantum dynamics for time-series processing.
AI.method: Using information processing capacity (a dynamical measure from nonlinear systems theory) to analyze quantum reservoir computing, placing diverse approaches (memory restriction, weak measurements, operation near quantum chaos edge, dissipative dynamics) in a unified framework.
AI.result: Identifies that apparently unrelated approaches are governed by the same underlying principle: tunable balance between memory retention and nonlinear response. Reveals regimes where quantum reservoirs surpass standard protocol and establishes fundamental connection between memory and nonlinear response.
AI.conclusion: Provides a general design principle for enhanced information processing in quantum reservoirs and enables systematic analysis and optimization inspired by classical dynamical quantifiers.

title: Experimental Quantum State Tomography of Multimode Gaussian States
summary: Multimode Gaussian states are a versatile resource for quantum information technologies and have been realized across a wide range of physical platforms. Recent progress in the large-scale generation of such states provides a key ingredient for scalable quantum technologies. Despite the importance of accurately characterizing these states, conventional tomography methods are often impractical because they require large sample sizes and can yield unphysical states. Here we present a reliable and efficient tomography method for multimode Gaussian states based on maximum-likelihood estimation. By directly operating on covariance matrices, the method avoids the exponential overhead associated with density-matrix reconstruction. We consider two commonly used detection schemes--single and joint homodyne detection--and systematically analyze the reconstruction performance. Our method outperforms conventional approaches by ensuring physical covariance matrices and achieving better agreement with the true states. To demonstrate the experimental applicability of the method, we experimentally generate various multipartite entangled states--six-mode graph states with different connectivity, a six-mode GHZ state, and a fully connected ten-mode graph state--and reconstruct their covariance matrices. Using the reconstructed covariance matrices, we quantify fidelities, detect entanglement, and reveal the multimode structure of squeezing and noise. Our technique offers a practical diagnostic tool for developing scalable quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: A maximum-likelihood tomography method for multimode Gaussian states that directly reconstructs covariance matrices, avoiding exponential overhead of density-matrix reconstruction, with experimental demonstration on multipartite entangled states.
AI.motivation: Multimode Gaussian states are important for quantum technologies but conventional tomography methods are impractical due to large sample requirements and potential unphysical results. There's a need for reliable and efficient characterization methods for large-scale Gaussian states.
AI.method: Maximum-likelihood estimation tomography that directly operates on covariance matrices rather than reconstructing full density matrices. The method considers both single and joint homodyne detection schemes and systematically analyzes reconstruction performance.
AI.result: The method outperforms conventional approaches by ensuring physical covariance matrices and achieving better agreement with true states. Experimental demonstration includes reconstruction of various multipartite entangled states: six-mode graph states with different connectivity, a six-mode GHZ state, and a fully connected ten-mode graph state.
AI.conclusion: The technique provides a practical diagnostic tool for developing scalable quantum technologies by enabling efficient and reliable characterization of multimode Gaussian states, with demonstrated experimental applicability for quantifying fidelities, detecting entanglement, and analyzing squeezing and noise structure.

title: Enhanced Emission from Boron-Vacancy Center in Rhombohedral Boron Nitride
summary: Various stacking combinations of the two-dimensional (2D) boron nitride (BN) honeycomb lattice can significantly modify the properties of the resulting 2D BN crystal. Here, we demonstrate through first-principles calculations that the brightness of the negatively charged boron-vacancy center (V$_\text{B}^{-}$) is enhanced by at least one order of magnitude in rhombohedral BN (rBN) compared to hexagonal BN (hBN), while the spin properties remain either comparable or even improved. This enhancement arises from the reduced symmetry of the crystal field in rBN. Our results suggest that room-temperature single-spin coherent control of V$_\text{B}^{-}$ is feasible in rBN, enabling its application as a single-spin quantum sensor in this 2D host. These findings demonstrate that engineered stacking of BN layers provides a powerful means to tailor the properties of embedded quantum defects.

AI.tldr: Rhombohedral BN stacking enhances V_B^- defect brightness by 10× while maintaining/improving spin properties, enabling room-temperature single-spin quantum sensing.
AI.motivation: To explore how different stacking arrangements of 2D boron nitride layers affect quantum defect properties, specifically the negatively charged boron-vacancy center (V_B^-), and to engineer improved quantum sensing platforms.
AI.method: First-principles calculations comparing rhombohedral BN (rBN) and hexagonal BN (hBN) stacking configurations, analyzing crystal field symmetry effects on V_B^- defect properties.
AI.result: V_B^- brightness enhanced by at least one order of magnitude in rBN compared to hBN, with spin properties either comparable or improved; reduced crystal field symmetry in rBN enables room-temperature single-spin coherent control.
AI.conclusion: Engineered stacking of BN layers provides a powerful method to tailor quantum defect properties, making rBN a promising host for single-spin quantum sensors with enhanced brightness and room-temperature operation.

title: High-yield integration design of fixed-frequency superconducting qubit systems using siZZle-CZ gates
summary: Fixed-frequency transmon qubits, characterized by simple architectures and long coherence times, are promising platforms for large-scale quantum computing. However, the rapidly increasing frequency collisions, which directly reduce the fabrication yield, hinder scaling, especially in cross-resonance (CR) gate-based architectures, wherein the restricted drive frequency severely limits the available design space. We investigate the Stark-induced ZZ by level excursions (siZZle) gate, which relaxes this limitation by allowing arbitrary drive-frequency choices. Extensive numerical analyses across a broad parameter range -- including the far-detuned regime that has received negligible prior attention -- reveal wide operating windows that support controlled-Z (CZ) fidelities >99.6%. Leveraging these windows, we design lattice architectures containing >1000 qubits, showing that even under 0.25% fabrication-induced frequency dispersion, the zero-collision yields in square and heavy-hexagonal lattices reach 80% and 100%, respectively. Thus, the siZZle-CZ gate is a scalable and collision-robust alternative to the CR gate, offering a viable route toward high-yield fixed-frequency transmon quantum processors.

AI.tldr: The siZZle-CZ gate enables high-fidelity quantum gates with arbitrary drive frequencies, overcoming frequency collision limitations in fixed-frequency transmon qubits and achieving high fabrication yields in large-scale architectures.
AI.motivation: Fixed-frequency transmon qubits face scaling challenges due to frequency collisions that reduce fabrication yield, especially in CR gate architectures where restricted drive frequencies limit design space.
AI.method: Investigated Stark-induced ZZ by level excursions (siZZle) gate allowing arbitrary drive frequencies, conducted extensive numerical analyses across broad parameter ranges including far-detuned regimes, and designed lattice architectures with >1000 qubits.
AI.result: Found wide operating windows supporting CZ fidelities >99.6%, achieved zero-collision yields of 80% in square lattices and 100% in heavy-hexagonal lattices under 0.25% fabrication-induced frequency dispersion.
AI.conclusion: The siZZle-CZ gate is a scalable, collision-robust alternative to CR gates, offering a viable route toward high-yield fixed-frequency transmon quantum processors.

title: Resonance-Suppression Principle for Prethermalization beyond Periodic Driving
comment: Main Text: 8 pages, 2 tables Supplemental: 56 pages, 2 tables, 5 figures
summary: Non-equilibrium dynamics of strongly and rapidly driven quantum many-body systems is poorly understood beyond periodic driving, where heating is exponentially slow in the drive frequency (Floquet Prethermalization). In contrast, non-periodic drives were found to exhibit widely different heating scalings with no unifying principle. This work identifies a resonance-suppression principle governing slow heating up to a prethermal lifetime $τ_*$: When the drive's spectral arithmetic structure restricts multiphoton resonances, $τ_*$ is controlled by low-frequency spectral suppression. The principle distinguishes (i) Single-photon suppression, quantified by a low-frequency suppression law $f(Ω)$ for the drive's Fourier Transform weight near $Ω=0$, from (ii) Multi-photon suppression, where nested commutators remain controlled if exceptional arithmetic structure satisfies a subadditive property. Remarkably, if multi-photon suppression holds, $τ_*$ scaling with drive speed $λ$ is governed by $f(Ω)$. This law of $τ_*$ is found through a small-divisor mechanism in this work's iterative rotating frame scheme. Multi-photon suppression breakdown separates $λ$-scaling of $τ_*$ in linear response and non-perturbative theory, shown by a case study of Quasi-Floquet driving. The principle is applied to (i) Resolve inconsistencies in literature on non-periodic driving, and (ii) Provide design principles for engineering prethermal phases of matter in programmable quantum simulators, exemplified by new non-periodic `Factorial' drives with tunable $τ_*$.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a resonance-suppression principle governing slow heating in non-periodically driven quantum many-body systems, distinguishing single-photon from multi-photon suppression mechanisms that control prethermal lifetimes.
AI.motivation: Non-equilibrium dynamics of strongly and rapidly driven quantum many-body systems is poorly understood beyond periodic driving. While periodic drives exhibit exponentially slow heating (Floquet Prethermalization), non-periodic drives show widely different heating scalings with no unifying principle.
AI.method: The work develops a resonance-suppression principle based on the drive's spectral arithmetic structure. It distinguishes single-photon suppression (quantified by low-frequency Fourier Transform suppression law f(Ω)) from multi-photon suppression (where nested commutators remain controlled if exceptional arithmetic structure satisfies subadditive property). Uses an iterative rotating frame scheme with small-divisor mechanism to derive the law for prethermal lifetime τ_*.
AI.result: Identifies that when multi-photon suppression holds, τ_* scaling with drive speed λ is governed by the low-frequency suppression law f(Ω). Shows multi-photon suppression breakdown separates λ-scaling of τ_* in linear response and non-perturbative theory. Applies principle to resolve inconsistencies in literature and provides design principles for engineering prethermal phases.
AI.conclusion: The resonance-suppression principle provides a unifying framework for understanding heating in non-periodically driven quantum systems. It enables engineering of prethermal phases in programmable quantum simulators through novel non-periodic 'Factorial' drives with tunable prethermal lifetimes.

title: Distilling the knowledge with quantum neural networks
summary: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) are a promising class of quantum machine learning models with potential quantum advantages when implemented on scalable, error-corrected quantum computers. However, as system sizes increase, deploying QNNs becomes challenging. Similar to their classical counterparts, a key obstacle to their practical applications is that large-scale QNNs may not be easily deployed on smaller systems that have limited resources. Here, we tackle this challenge by compressing QNNs via knowledge distillation. We demonstrate how well-trained QNNs on large systems can be distilled into smaller architectures with similar configurations. We numerically show that knowledge distillation helps reduce the training cost of QNNs in terms of the number of qubits and circuit depth. Additionally, we find that a self-knowledge-distillation approach can accelerate training convergence. We believe our results offer new strategies for the efficient compression and practical deployment of QNNs.

AI.tldr: QNN compression via knowledge distillation enables deployment of large quantum models on smaller systems by reducing qubit requirements and circuit depth while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Large-scale Quantum Neural Networks face deployment challenges on resource-constrained quantum systems, similar to classical neural networks. The need exists for compression techniques to enable practical QNN applications on smaller quantum hardware.
AI.method: Knowledge distillation approach where well-trained QNNs on large systems are compressed into smaller architectures with similar configurations. Includes both standard knowledge distillation and self-knowledge-distillation techniques.
AI.result: Knowledge distillation reduces QNN training costs in terms of qubit count and circuit depth. Self-knowledge-distillation accelerates training convergence. Numerical demonstrations show effective compression while maintaining performance.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge distillation offers viable strategies for efficient QNN compression and practical deployment, addressing scalability challenges in quantum machine learning.

title: Single-Trajectory Gibbs Sampling for Non-Commuting Observables
summary:
Estimating thermal expectation values of quantum many-body systems is a central challenge in physics, chemistry, and materials science. Standard quantum Gibbs sampling protocols address this task by preparing the Gibbs state from scratch after every measurement, incurring a full mixing-time cost at each step. Recent advances in single-trajectory Gibbs sampling \cite{jiang2026} substantially reduce this overhead: once stationarity is reached, measurements can be collected along a single trajectory without re-thermalizing, provided the measurement channel preserves the Gibbs ensemble. However, explicit constructions of such non-destructive measurements have been limited primarily to observables that commute with the Hamiltonian. In this work, we fundamentally extend the single-trajectory framework to arbitrary, non-commuting observables. We provide two measurement constructions that extract measurement information without fully destroying the Gibbs state, thereby eliminating the need for full re-mixing between samples.
  First, we construct a measurement that satisfies exact detailed balance. This ensures the system remains in equilibrium throughout the trajectory, allowing measurement outcomes to decorrelate in an autocorrelation time that could be significantly shorter than the global mixing time. Second, assuming the underlying quantum Gibbs sampler has a positive spectral gap, we design a simplified measurement scheme that ensures the post-selected state serves as a warm start for rapid re-mixing. This approach successfully decouples the resampling cost from the global mixing time. Both measurement schemes admit efficient quantum circuit implementations, requiring only polylogarithmic Hamiltonian simulation time.

AI.tldr: Single-trajectory Gibbs sampling extended to arbitrary non-commuting observables via two measurement constructions that avoid full re-thermalization between samples.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum Gibbs sampling requires full re-thermalization after each measurement, incurring mixing-time overhead. Existing single-trajectory methods only work for commuting observables, limiting practical applications.
AI.method: Two measurement constructions: 1) Exact detailed balance measurement that preserves equilibrium throughout trajectory, 2) Simplified scheme using post-selected states as warm starts for rapid re-mixing when sampler has positive spectral gap.
AI.result: Both schemes decouple resampling cost from global mixing time, enabling efficient sampling of arbitrary observables. They admit efficient quantum circuit implementations with polylogarithmic Hamiltonian simulation time.
AI.conclusion: Fundamentally extends single-trajectory Gibbs sampling to non-commuting observables, eliminating key bottleneck in quantum thermal expectation value estimation.

title: Systematic construction of digital autonomous quantum error correction for state preparation and error suppression via conditional Gaussian operations
summary: In continuous-variable quantum computing, autonomous quantum error correction (QEC) can dissipatively steer a noisy quantum state into a target state or manifold, enabling robust quantum information processing without explicit syndrome measurements and feedback. Here, we propose a nullifier-based digital autonomous QEC enabled by conditional Gaussian operations. By designing jump operators for target nullifiers and compiling the resulting Lindbladian into a Trotterized sequence of elementary conditional Gaussian operations, we demonstrate two use cases: (i) deterministic preparation of non-Gaussian resource states for universal computation, including finitely squeezed cubic phase states and approximate trisqueezed states, and (ii) autonomous suppression of dephasing error for cat and squeezed cat states. We provide explicit gate decompositions for the required conditional Gaussian operations and numerically evaluate the performance under realistic imperfections, including photon loss in the bosonic mode and ancillary-qubit decoherence. Our results clarify the resource requirements and trade-offs, such as circuit depth, time-step choices, and the required set of conditional Gaussian operations, for scalable, gate-level implementations of autonomous state preparation and error suppression.

AI.tldr: Digital autonomous quantum error correction using conditional Gaussian operations for preparing non-Gaussian resource states and suppressing dephasing errors in continuous-variable systems.
AI.motivation: Autonomous quantum error correction can dissipatively steer noisy quantum states into target states without explicit syndrome measurements and feedback, enabling robust quantum information processing in continuous-variable systems.
AI.method: Nullifier-based digital autonomous QEC using conditional Gaussian operations; designing jump operators for target nullifiers and compiling Lindbladian into Trotterized sequences of elementary conditional Gaussian operations.
AI.result: Demonstrated deterministic preparation of non-Gaussian resource states (finitely squeezed cubic phase states, approximate trisqueezed states) and autonomous suppression of dephasing error for cat and squeezed cat states; provided explicit gate decompositions and evaluated performance under realistic imperfections.
AI.conclusion: Clarified resource requirements and trade-offs (circuit depth, time-step choices, required conditional Gaussian operations) for scalable, gate-level implementations of autonomous state preparation and error suppression in continuous-variable quantum computing.

title: Neural network approach to mitigating intra-gate crosstalk in superconducting CZ gates
summary:
The potential of quantum computing is fundamentally constrained by the inherent susceptibility of qubits to noise and crosstalk, particularly during multi-qubit gate operations.
  Existing strategies, such as hardware isolation and dynamical decoupling, face limitations in scalability, experimental feasibility, and robustness against complex noise sources.
  In this manuscript, we propose a physics-guided neural control (PGNC) framework to generate robust control pulses for superconducting transmon qubit systems, specifically targeting crosstalk mitigation.
  By combining a hardware aware parameterization with a Hamiltonian-informed objective that accounts for condition-dependent crosstalk distortions, PGNC steers the search toward smooth and physically realizable pulses while efficiently exploring high dimensional control landscapes.
  Numerical simulations for the CZ gate demonstrate superior fidelity and pulse smoothness compared to a Krotov baseline under matched constraints.
  Taken together, the results show consistent and practically meaningful improvements in both nominal and perturbed conditions, with pronounced gains in worst-case fidelity, supporting PGNC as a viable route to robust control on near-term transmon devices.

AI.tldr: Physics-guided neural control (PGNC) framework generates robust control pulses for superconducting transmon qubits, specifically targeting crosstalk mitigation, with demonstrated superior fidelity and pulse smoothness compared to Krotov methods.
AI.motivation: Quantum computing faces fundamental constraints from qubit susceptibility to noise and crosstalk during multi-qubit gate operations. Existing strategies like hardware isolation and dynamical decoupling have limitations in scalability, experimental feasibility, and robustness against complex noise sources.
AI.method: Proposes a physics-guided neural control (PGNC) framework combining hardware-aware parameterization with Hamiltonian-informed objective that accounts for condition-dependent crosstalk distortions. PGNC steers search toward smooth, physically realizable pulses while efficiently exploring high-dimensional control landscapes.
AI.result: Numerical simulations for CZ gate demonstrate superior fidelity and pulse smoothness compared to Krotov baseline under matched constraints. Results show consistent improvements in both nominal and perturbed conditions, with pronounced gains in worst-case fidelity.
AI.conclusion: PGNC represents a viable route to robust control on near-term transmon devices, offering practical improvements for crosstalk mitigation in superconducting qubit systems.

title: Gate-based Readout and Cooling of Neutral Atoms
summary: Neutral atom arrays have seen tremendous progress in quantum simulation, quantum metrology, and fault-tolerant quantum computing. However, hardware constraints such as atom loss and heating remain significant challenges. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive ancilla-based toolbox for optical tweezer experiments that utilizes high-fidelity Rydberg entangling gates and ancilla atoms to mitigate these physical limitations. First, we demonstrate repeated ancilla-based atom readout, achieving improved detection fidelity over multiple rounds with minimal perturbation to data atoms. Second, leveraging the quantized motional states in tweezer-trapped strontium atoms, we transduce quantum information from the electronic to the motional manifold. This enables us to perform mid-circuit ancilla-based atom loss detection in a coherence-preserving fashion. Finally, we demonstrate algorithmic cooling, a circuit-based sequence that deterministically cools data atoms by transferring their motional entropy to the electronic states of ancilla atoms. We observe a marked reduction in the atomic temperature of data atoms. These tools offer a pathway to continuous operation in tweezer clocks and complement recent developments in continuous reloading experiments.

AI.tldr: Ancilla-based toolbox for optical tweezer experiments using Rydberg gates and ancilla atoms to mitigate hardware constraints like atom loss and heating, enabling improved readout, loss detection, and algorithmic cooling.
AI.motivation: Neutral atom arrays face hardware constraints including atom loss and heating that limit quantum simulation, metrology, and computing applications. There is a need for techniques to mitigate these physical limitations while preserving quantum coherence.
AI.method: Developed ancilla-based toolbox using high-fidelity Rydberg entangling gates and ancilla atoms in optical tweezer experiments with strontium atoms. Methods include: 1) repeated ancilla-based atom readout, 2) transduction of quantum information from electronic to motional manifolds using quantized motional states, 3) mid-circuit ancilla-based atom loss detection, and 4) algorithmic cooling circuits that transfer motional entropy from data atoms to ancilla electronic states.
AI.result: Achieved improved detection fidelity over multiple readout rounds with minimal perturbation to data atoms; demonstrated coherence-preserving mid-circuit atom loss detection; observed marked reduction in atomic temperature of data atoms through algorithmic cooling.
AI.conclusion: The ancilla-based toolbox provides effective mitigation of hardware constraints in neutral atom arrays, offering a pathway to continuous operation in tweezer clocks and complementing continuous reloading experiments for enhanced quantum information processing capabilities.

title: Efficient Gaussian Simulations of Fermionic Open Quantum Systems
comment: 8 figures; 34 pages; to appear in Adv. Quant. Tech
summary: We review existing classical simulation methods for performing fermionic Gaussian operations and develop new methods to address the gap by adhering to the fundamental theoretical framework established by Bravyi [Quantum Info. Comput. 5, 216 (2005)] for the most general fermionic Gaussian processes. Throughout this attempt, the focus remains on the unified approach that can be applied to generic fermionic Gaussian operations. This is beneficial since the selection of simulation methods has often been based on an ad hoc choice, heavily influenced by the specific model and circumstances, rather than on a systematic approach.

AI.tldr: Review and development of classical simulation methods for fermionic Gaussian operations based on Bravyi's theoretical framework, emphasizing a unified systematic approach over ad hoc methods.
AI.motivation: Existing simulation methods for fermionic Gaussian operations lack systematic approaches and rely heavily on ad hoc choices influenced by specific models and circumstances, rather than following a unified theoretical framework.
AI.method: Review existing classical simulation methods and develop new methods adhering to Bravyi's fundamental theoretical framework for general fermionic Gaussian processes, focusing on a unified approach applicable to generic fermionic Gaussian operations.
AI.result: Development of new simulation methods that address gaps in existing approaches by systematically applying Bravyi's theoretical framework to fermionic Gaussian operations.
AI.conclusion: A unified systematic approach based on Bravyi's theoretical framework provides a more robust foundation for simulating fermionic Gaussian operations compared to existing ad hoc methods.

title: Implemetation of a shooting technique for quantum optimal control on spin qudits
summary: High-fidelity control of quantum systems is essential for scalable quantum technologies. We introduce a shooting-based quantum optimal control algorithm for systems of finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, and demonstrate its performances through numerical simulations on systems inspired from single molecule magnets. Our method efficiently decomposes quantum gates into selective electromagnetic pulses, outperforming the standard GRAPE method against which it is benchmarked, especially in larger Hilbert spaces

AI.tldr: A shooting-based quantum optimal control algorithm outperforms GRAPE for decomposing quantum gates into electromagnetic pulses, especially in larger Hilbert spaces, with demonstrations on single-molecule magnet systems.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity control of quantum systems is essential for scalable quantum technologies, requiring efficient methods to decompose quantum gates into selective electromagnetic pulses.
AI.method: A shooting-based quantum optimal control algorithm for finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, benchmarked against the standard GRAPE method, with numerical simulations on systems inspired from single molecule magnets.
AI.result: The method outperforms GRAPE, especially in larger Hilbert spaces, demonstrating efficient decomposition of quantum gates into selective electromagnetic pulses.
AI.conclusion: The shooting-based quantum optimal control algorithm provides superior performance for quantum gate decomposition compared to standard GRAPE, offering improved control fidelity for scalable quantum technologies.

title: All-optical quantum memory using bosonic quantum error correction codes
summary: Reliable quantum memory is essential for scalable quantum networks and fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing. We present a quantitative analysis of an all-optical quantum memory architecture in which a Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) encoded qubit is stored in a fibre loop and periodically stabilized using teleportation-based error correction. By modelling fibre propagation as a pure-loss channel and representing each correction round as an effective logical map acting on the Bloch vector, we obtain a compact description of the full multi-round memory channel. We show that syndrome decoder optimization plays a crucial role in the experimentally relevant finite-squeezing regime. The optimal decoder deviates from standard square-grid GKP decoder in both tile-size and tile-shape, leading to significant improved logical performance. Using this optimized decoding strategy, we identify a squeezing-dependent optimal spacing between correction nodes that maximizes the memory lifetime. Remarkably, this optimal segment length is largely independent of the desired storage time, providing a simple and practical design rule for fibre-loop quantum memory. We further find a squeezing threshold of approximately 6.7 dB below which intermediate error correction becomes counterproductive, while above threshold the achievable storage time increases approximately exponentially with squeezing. For example, at 17 dB squeezing, storage times exceeding 400 ms can be achieved with logical infidelity below 1%. These results establish clear performance benchmarks and reveal the fundamental trade-off between photon loss, squeezing, and correction frequency in continuous-variable architectures. Our findings provide actionable design principles for near-term photonic quantum memory and clarify the path toward scalable all-optical fault-tolerant quantum storage.

AI.tldr: Analysis of an all-optical quantum memory using GKP-encoded qubits in fiber loops with teleportation-based error correction, showing optimal decoder design and squeezing-dependent performance thresholds.
AI.motivation: Reliable quantum memory is essential for scalable quantum networks and fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, requiring architectures that can effectively combat photon loss in optical systems.
AI.method: Quantitative analysis of an all-optical quantum memory architecture where GKP-encoded qubits are stored in fiber loops and periodically stabilized using teleportation-based error correction. Fiber propagation is modeled as a pure-loss channel, with each correction round represented as an effective logical map on the Bloch vector, enabling compact description of the multi-round memory channel.
AI.result: Syndrome decoder optimization is crucial in finite-squeezing regime, with optimal decoder deviating from standard square-grid GKP decoder in both tile-size and shape, leading to significant performance improvements. Squeezing threshold of ~6.7 dB identified below which intermediate error correction becomes counterproductive. Above threshold, storage time increases approximately exponentially with squeezing (e.g., 17 dB squeezing achieves >400 ms storage with <1% logical infidelity). Optimal segment length between correction nodes is largely independent of desired storage time.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes clear performance benchmarks and reveals fundamental trade-offs between photon loss, squeezing, and correction frequency in continuous-variable architectures. Provides actionable design principles for near-term photonic quantum memory and clarifies path toward scalable all-optical fault-tolerant quantum storage.

title: Neural Belief-Matching Decoding for Topological Quantum Error Correction Codes
summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) is critical for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing. Topological codes, such as the toric code, offer hardware-efficient architectures but their Tanner graphs contain many girth-4 cycles that degrade the performance of belief-propagation (BP) decoding. For this reason, BP decoding is typically followed by a more complex second stage decoder such as minimum-weight perfect matching. These combined decoders achieve a remarkable performance, albeit at the cost of increased complexity. In this paper we propose two key improvements for the decoding of toric code. The first one is replacing the BP decoder by a neural BP decoder, giving rise to the neural belief-matching decoder which substantially decreases the average decoding complexity. The main drawback of this approach is the high cost associated with the training of the neural BP decoder. To address this issue, we impose a convolutional architecture on the neural BP decoder, enabling weight sharing across the spatially homogeneous structure of the code's factor graph. This design allows a model trained on a modest-size topological code to be directly transferred to much larger instances, preserving decoding quality while dramatically lowering the training burden. Our numerical experiments on toric-code lattices of various sizes demonstrate that this technique does not result in a noticeable loss in performance.

AI.tldr: Neural belief-matching decoder with convolutional architecture enables efficient transfer learning for toric code decoding, reducing training burden while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Topological codes like toric codes have girth-4 cycles that degrade BP decoding performance, requiring complex second-stage decoders. Current combined decoders achieve good performance but at high complexity. There's a need for more efficient decoding approaches that reduce complexity while maintaining performance.
AI.method: Proposes two improvements: 1) Replace BP decoder with neural BP decoder to create neural belief-matching decoder, reducing average decoding complexity. 2) Impose convolutional architecture on neural BP decoder to enable weight sharing across the spatially homogeneous factor graph structure, allowing transfer learning from small to large code instances.
AI.result: The convolutional neural BP decoder enables models trained on modest-size topological codes to be directly transferred to much larger instances without noticeable performance loss. This dramatically lowers training burden while preserving decoding quality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed neural belief-matching decoder with convolutional architecture provides an efficient solution for toric code decoding that reduces both decoding complexity and training burden through transfer learning, making it practical for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Model selection in hybrid quantum neural networks with applications to quantum transformer architectures
summary: Quantum machine learning models generally lack principled design guidelines, often requiring full resource-intensive training across numerous choices of encodings, quantum circuit designs and initialization strategies to find effective configuration. To address this challenge, we develope the Quantum Bias-Expressivity Toolbox ($\texttt{QBET}$), a framework for evaluating quantum, classical, and hybrid transformer architectures. In this toolbox, we introduce lean metrics for Simplicity Bias ($\texttt{SB}$) and Expressivity ($\texttt{EXP}$), for comparing across various models, and extend the analysis of $\texttt{SB}$ to generative and multiclass-classification tasks. We show that $\texttt{QBET}$ enables efficient pre-screening of promising model variants obviating the need to execute complete training pipelines. In evaluations on transformer-based classification and generative tasks we employ a total of $18$ qubits for embeddings ($6$ qubits each for query, key, and value). We identify scenarios in which quantum self-attention variants surpass their classical counterparts by ranking the respective models according to the $\texttt{SB}$ metric and comparing their relative performance.

AI.tldr: QBET is a framework for evaluating quantum, classical, and hybrid transformer architectures using lean metrics for Simplicity Bias (SB) and Expressivity (EXP), enabling efficient pre-screening of model variants without full training.
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning models lack principled design guidelines, requiring resource-intensive training across numerous choices of encodings, quantum circuit designs, and initialization strategies to find effective configurations.
AI.method: Developed Quantum Bias-Expressivity Toolbox (QBET) with metrics for Simplicity Bias (SB) and Expressivity (EXP), extended SB analysis to generative and multiclass-classification tasks, evaluated transformer-based classification and generative tasks using 18 qubits for embeddings (6 qubits each for query, key, and value).
AI.result: QBET enables efficient pre-screening of promising model variants, identifying scenarios where quantum self-attention variants surpass classical counterparts by ranking models according to SB metric and comparing relative performance.
AI.conclusion: The QBET framework provides a systematic approach for evaluating quantum transformer architectures, reducing the need for full training pipelines by offering principled metrics for comparing model variants across quantum, classical, and hybrid designs.

title: Global Optimization for Parametrized Quantum Circuits
summary: In the absence of error correction, noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices are operated by training parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs) so as to minimize a suitable loss function. Finding the optimal parameters of those circuits is a hard optimization problem, where global guarantees are known only for highly structured cases of limited practical relevance, and first-order methods can fail to find even local minima due to the presence of barren plateaus. In this work, we study the training of practical classes of PQCs, namely polynomial-depth circuits with a constant number of trainable parameters. This captures widely used PQC families, including fixed-depth QAOA, hardware-efficient ansätze, and Fixed Parameter Count QAOA. Our main technical result is a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (FPRAS), which, for every $ε>0$, returns an $ε$-approximate solution to the problem's global optimum with high probability, and has runtime and query complexity polynomial in $1/ε$ and the number of qubits. Unlike the standard hybrid quantum-classical training loop in variational algorithms, where the quantum device is queried repeatedly throughout the training, our approach separates the computation into two distinct stages: (1) an initial quantum data-acquisition phase, followed by (2) a classical global-optimization phase based on the trigonometric moment/sum-of-squares hierarchies. Under a standard flat-extension condition, which can be checked numerically, the method also supports the extraction of optimal circuit parameters. The existence of an FPRAS implies that the promise problem associated with the optimization of poly-depth constant-parameter PQC is in BQP. This imposes a limitation on the expressive power of the class, namely, it cannot encode combinatorial optimization problems whose objective values are separated by an inverse-polynomial gap.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an FPRAS (fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme) for training polynomial-depth quantum circuits with constant parameters, separating quantum data acquisition from classical optimization.
AI.motivation: Current variational quantum algorithms face challenges in training parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs) due to barren plateaus and lack of global guarantees, making optimization difficult for practical quantum devices.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: (1) quantum data-acquisition phase to collect measurement data, followed by (2) classical global-optimization phase using trigonometric moment/sum-of-squares hierarchies. The method provides an FPRAS with polynomial runtime in 1/ε and qubit count.
AI.result: Demonstrates that training polynomial-depth circuits with constant parameters admits an FPRAS, placing the associated promise problem in BQP. This imposes limitations on the expressive power of such circuits for combinatorial optimization.
AI.conclusion: The existence of an FPRAS for training practical PQC classes provides theoretical guarantees for optimization and reveals fundamental limitations on what problems such circuits can efficiently encode and solve.

title: Using spatiotemporal Born rule for testing macroscopic realism: some applications to the pseudo-density matrices and nonclassical temporal correlations
summary: We show that, given an evolving quantum system and the quasiprobability distribution generated by the spatiotemporal generalization of the Born rule in pseudo density-matrices (PDMs), this distribution deviates from the sequential measurements probability distribution, given by the Lüders von-Neumann distribution, if and only if the non-signaling in time (NSIT) is violated; equivalently, if and only if the macroscopic realism (MR) is violated. Furthermore, we propose a definition of temporal entanglement according to the structure of the PDMs that is analogous to the definition of spatial entanglement in density matrices, showing that temporal entanglement is necessary for the violation of temporal Bell inequalities and the violation of MR. We employ our results to study the relationship between the negativity of the PDM, temporal entanglement, violation of temporal Bell inequalities, and MR.

AI.tldr: PDM quasiprobability distributions deviate from sequential measurement probabilities when NSIT is violated, equivalent to MR violation; temporal entanglement defined via PDM structure is necessary for temporal Bell inequality violations and MR violations.
AI.motivation: To establish connections between pseudo density-matrix (PDM) quasiprobability distributions, sequential measurement probabilities, non-signaling in time (NSIT), macroscopic realism (MR), temporal entanglement, and temporal Bell inequalities.
AI.method: Analyze PDM quasiprobability distributions and compare with Lüders von-Neumann sequential measurement distributions; define temporal entanglement based on PDM structure analogous to spatial entanglement in density matrices; study relationships between PDM negativity, temporal entanglement, temporal Bell inequality violations, and MR violations.
AI.result: PDM distributions deviate from sequential measurement distributions if and only if NSIT is violated (equivalently, MR is violated); temporal entanglement is necessary for temporal Bell inequality violations and MR violations; relationships established between PDM negativity, temporal entanglement, and these violations.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes fundamental connections between PDM quasiprobabilities, temporal correlations, and quantum temporal phenomena, showing that temporal entanglement plays a crucial role in violations of temporal Bell inequalities and macroscopic realism.

title: Fiber-optic quantum interface with an array of more than 100 individually addressable atoms on an optical nanofiber
summary: Integrating the scalability of individually addressable arrays of optical-tweezer-trapped single atoms with the efficient light-matter interface provided by nanophotonic waveguides has been a long-standing challenge in quantum technologies based on atoms and photons. Here we realize a quantum interface between photons guided in an optical nanofiber with a diameter of 310 nm and an array of on average 155 individually addressable atoms. Using a spatial light modulator and an objective lens with NA = 0.45, single cesium atoms are trapped in a one-dimensional array of 200 optical tweezer spots with micrometer-scale trap sizes on the nanofiber. Individual atoms are addressed by spatially scanning an excitation laser beam, focused to a spot size comparable to that of the traps through the same objective lens, along the nanofiber. We confirm the single-atom nature of the individual trapping sites through photon-correlation measurements of the guided fluorescence, observing strong photon antibunching with $g^{(2)}(0) \approx 0.26$. We measure trap lifetimes of a few hundred milliseconds, with a maximum value of 460 ms, at an atom-surface separation of 670 nm without active cooling, representing an order-of-magnitude improvement over previous nanofiber traps.
